Script: #Zumamustfall

VO: 22”
For the past week and a half the Zuma must fall hashtag dominated social media– precipitated by the calamitous decision last Wednesday evening to sack finance Minister Nanhlanha Nene and replace him with backbencher David van Rooyen. The social media fallout was immediate say communications strategist Sarah Britten.

Sarah:
I saw that first tweet come through and I realized that oh boy we were in for something. And I started watching the reactions and it was like watching South Africa process it’s emotional collective self.

VO: 5”
South Africans took to social media to make sense of the shock decision.

Sarah:
What was great about twitter in particular was that you had everyone from political leaders, business leaders, economists, to ordinary people in the street all expressing their views on this.

VO: 6”
Power FM radio DJ Lawrence Hlabane was preparing to go on air when the news broke.

Lawrence:
We had to lead with the story and on my show we have an open line in the evening and then that’s how we started and the response was immediate.

Devi:
What were ordinary South African’s saying?

Lawrence:
Well I think the tone of Zuma must go it was already starting and a lot of people were saying what else are we waiting for - this was like a final straw.

VO:
Here’s a sample.

Upsound:
Power 98.7

Podcasts:
The president what it says in terms of – now we can see who comes first its not the country.

Are they making decisions that are going to benefit us as a nation or they are making decisions only to benefit one of two?

Devi:
Were any of them defenders of Jacob Zuma on your show?

Lawrence:
No…I can’t think of any.

VO: 8”
Social media was abuzz and by the weekend the hashtag dominated timelines and conversations says media monitoring expert Tonya Koury.

Tonya:
It’s bigger than the opening day of the Oscar Pistorius trial and most days of the Oscar Pistorius trial. And we have never seen a story bigger than Oscar Pistorius in the history of our monitoring.

Devi link
The thing about social media is that it is an open line to the rest of the world. Everyone can tap into the conversation and they did.

VO: 9”
There have been 500 000 tweets on the issue alone but in terms of unique perspectives the number was sitting at 120 000 earlier this week.

Tonya:
It’s the number of actual unique items that have been put out there from the consumer’s perspective in the social media community

VO 6”
The conversation didn’t just go viral it went global too as this heat map shows.

Tonya:
So South Africa is obviously where the most heat is coming from…

Devi:
But they are talking about us everywhere!!!

Tonya
Everywhere, everywhere. You’ll see the darker the shade of red the more heat there is.

VO: 3”
A conversation that put the spotlight firmly on our currency.

Sarah
It suggests that the people doing the trading are watching the news reports, they are watching social media and its having a viral effect. It’s increasing the propensity to act in a certain way.

VO: 3”
And yet the ANC’s silence was deafening.

Lawrence:
There was a vacuum it was if the country had gone into a coma – until two days later that we are starting to see that there’s still signs of leadership.

VO: 15
During this vacuum, some big names broke ranks. Shaka sisulu tweeted:

“I’m going to be an ass and break ranks with most of my comades’ utterences. I don’t agree with last night’s sudden cabinet reshuffle.”

VO:
It was significant says political commentator Ranjeni Musamy.

Ranjeni:
It’s come to a time where people of good conscience have to speak up. A person like Shaka Sisulu comes from a pedigree of ANC leaders. He is a big name in the organization. So its not insignificant.

Sarah:
It made mainstream news, it was on all the news websites. So twitter in particular becomes news very quickly and in turn that feeds the discussion and so it goes.

VO: 12”
Barbara Hogan’s comments spread like wildfire and gained traction online.
Gauteng education MEC Panyaza Lesufi reportedly voiced his dissent on Minister Nene’s removal on Facebook.

“I don’t agree. #No”

Ranjeni:
He’s one person in a position of power but all he did is condemn the removal of former minister Nene. He has not condemned the irresponsibility of the president. He has not condemned other people sitting by quietly and watching this happen.

VO: 6”
To date no-one from the 80 member National Executive council has dared to speak up.

Devi:
Even though the rand was in free fall in true SA fashion we managed to keep our sense of humour.

Sarah:
We’ve always responded with humour to dramatic events so its natural that we’re going to go onto social media in particular to share our feelings.

VO:
Donald Trump is currently topping the international charts at 60%. But in Trumps case it’s just his hair and not the dollar that’s in freefall. Inevitably parody accounts also surfaced on social media – like short lived minister van Rooyen’s.

Sarah:
Parody accounts are usually the first things that pop up in response to news events. This is true of everywhere in the world and it was really funny to see who was taken in by it - Tony Leon believed it was real!

VO: 8”
Even the rand had its own twitter account and the weekend special minister fast became the butt of many jokes.

Tonya:
We saw a hashtag come out #vanrooyendidnoteven and that was like – get the pin code to the ATM machine, take a selfie at his desk, get the Wifi password. That’s South Africans though we always make light of a crisis situation.

VO:
But jokes aside – social media is a recognized catalyst for change – take the Arab Spring for example.

Sarah:
The reason social media did play a role was that it allowed different social actors who were separated and who generally could not connect with each it allowed them to connect with each other. So in that sense social media is very powerful and its why oppressive governments like to keep it under control.

VO: 6”
In Brazil social media galvanised support to impeach president Dilma Rousseff.

Sarah
Brazilians marched and they succeeded but I don’t think South Africans are in a space where they are willing to do the same.

Devi link
One of the criticisms against the #Zumamustfall social media campaign and the marches is that it reflects a white racist point of view. But is that the case?

Lawrence:
The audience here its more of the working class but you also find the middle and upper class. The myth that only whites are whingers in this country – I think its a myth.

VO: 5”
The race card remains Zuma’s best defence mechanism. It’s a case of divide and rule.

Sarah:
The more racist views you see being shared the more likelihood that support for Jacob Zuma will be shored up. White racism in fact his best weapon.

VO: 18
It was a seminal moment in our history when on Wednesday, on reconciliation day, South African’s gathered at several venues around the country adding to the groundswell of the Zuma must fall campaign. The biggest march took place at the iconic Nelson Mandela Bridge.

Devi link:
South Africans have come out in their droves to support the Zuma must fall campaign. But the burning question is this the tipping point, is enough to bring change in SA?

VO: 3”
Social justice activist Mark Heywood was one of the organisers.

Mark:
It’s clear that there’ a mood in the country: there’s a mood of anger, there is a mood of despair, but there is also a mood where people want change and they want to come together to create change.

VO: 4”
Around 4000 people gathered to add their voices.

Voxies

We want out monies that was spent on Nkandla!
It’s not about white people, its not about black people, or any race or agenda or any specific culture, it’s just about South Africa taking its country back.

VO
And former trade unionist Zwelinzima Vavi didn’t hold back.

Vavi:
To the president and to all those who give him the round of applause. We are enough! We are gatvol! We cannot take it anymore.

VO: 5”
At the Union buildings in Pretoria around 2000 disgruntled citizens gathered.

Voxies

He should be out from the ANC – he is not a leader. He’s not a man who can run a country.
The ANC shown they don’t have the balls to take control of the situation.
And I think we should also vote differently at the next election.

VO: 6”
And in Cape Town the organizer are sure that this is the first of many gatherings where South African’s would take a stand.

Msizi:
As more people get galvanized, mobilized, you are going to see this growing more and more. This is the first of many to come.

VO: 8
In the midst of the marches the Zuma must fall hashtag rose from 70% of to nearly 90% on social media- its unprecedented.

Lawrence:
This was a moment that can never be ignored. I don’t think the politics of the ANC can remain the same after this.

VO:
Social media is a dipstick and amplifier of public opinion – but it’s only when it translates to boots on the ground, posters held high and voices ringing through the air – that real change will come.

Mark:
We’ve reached a point in this country where with the crisis in health, with the crisis in education, the levels of corruption and really with the contempt of the president for the people of this country its becoming a tipping point. People are saying not in my name anymore.


Promo 1:

VO: 4
The Zuma must fall hashtag has dominated social media.

Tonya:
Bigger than the Oscar trial

VO: 3
We ask will social media drive political change?



Promo 2:

VO: 9”
With the rand in free fall in the midst of the shock decision to sack finance minister Nene – South African’s took satire to a new level on social media.

Sarah:


Promo 3:

VO: 6
The Zuma must fall social media campaign saw South Africans taking their tweets to the streets.

Lawrence

VO;
Will it bring change?
